query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The creep resistance of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by the formation of uniformly distributed, coherent nanoscale precipitates at the interfaces between FCC and BCC phases, which effectively impede dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding under continuous loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FCC/BCC HEA protective coating with a heterogeneous microstructure and non-uniform distribution of secondary phase particles or precipitates.
generation.intervention: A heat treatment designed to promote the nucleation and uniform dispersion of coherent nanoscale precipitates (e.g., ordered B2 or L1₂ type) preferentially at the FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Continuous high temperature and sustained stress conditions that activate creep mechanisms, particularly dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent nanoscale precipitates at the FCC/BCC phase boundaries, which serve as pinning sites for dislocations.
generation.mechanism: Uniformly distributed, coherent precipitates at the interfaces create obstacles to dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding by raising the local activation energy for these processes, thereby reducing the overall creep rate of the coating under continuous loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Heat-treated coatings with a uniform and coherent precipitate distribution will exhibit significantly reduced creep rates, higher creep activation energies, and longer times to failure compared to as-deposited coatings with a heterogeneous microstructure.
generation.baseline: As-deposited coatings with inhomogeneous precipitate distribution and weak phase boundary pinning, resulting in higher creep rates under continuous loading.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be effective under sustained high-temperature and high-stress conditions where dislocation climb and grain boundary sliding dominate the creep deformation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal size, spacing, and coherency of the precipitates required for maximum creep resistance are not well defined and may vary with overall alloy composition and specific test conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FCC/BCC HEA protective coatings: one set remains as-deposited, while the other undergoes a tailored heat treatment aimed at producing a uniform distribution of coherent nanoscale precipitates at the phase boundaries. Subject both sets to identical continuous creep tests at an elevated temperature under a constant load.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves to extract steady-state creep rates
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to quantify precipitate size, distribution, and coherency at FCC/BCC interfaces
Determination of creep activation energy via temperature-dependent testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and an increase in creep activation energy relative to the as-deposited coatings, the proposed role of coherent interphase precipitates in controlling creep resistance will be refuted.

Question: What are the creep deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution characteristics of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy in the intermediate temperature range of 500–600 °C?. System: Equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn20 (atomic percentage) FCC-structured high-entropy alloy. Processing: Vacuum induction melting with 99.9 mass% purity elements, re-melted five times, drop-cast, homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled 40%, and annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: Tensile creep tests at 500, 550, and 600 °C under applied stresses of 140–400 MPa; interrupted tests at steady-state stages cooled with liquid nitrogen.
